themes.title: Explore themes
themes.concept: A Flint theme is a formal specification that shapes a chart throughout its creation. It influences the compiler at three levels.

layout.title: Layout algorithm
layout.body: Changes how the compiler allocates space and relates elements. It controls density and breathing room, and decides when labels, legends, axes, and annotations move, appear, or give way.

semantics.title: Semantic roles
semantics.body: Sets presentation rules by meaning. Field roles, order, groups, and hierarchy drive contrast, emphasis, series identity, and representation.

identity.title: Geometry and typography
identity.body: Defines type, color, surfaces, line weight, corners, and mark shapes. Together, these choices give every chart a consistent brand.

themes.generalization: Because these rules are global, they work across chart types, data shapes, and canvas sizes. Add a chart or change the data, and the compiler carries the same behavior and identity forward.

landing.heroTitle: Flint: A Visualization Language for the AI Era
landing.installMcp: For agents, use the <mcpLink>MCP server</mcpLink>; see the <skillLink>Agent Skill</skillLink> for standalone guidance.
landing.installGallery: Explore {{chartTypes}} chart types and {{examples}} examples in the <galleryLink>gallery</galleryLink>.
landing.themeLead: Flint employs a formal theme specification so designers can encode visual decisions once and apply them coherently across every chart in a library, creating a consistent and recognizable brand.

release040.text: Flint 0.4.0 adds 38 Plotly chart types and 18 native, editable Excel chart templates.

dynamicWidgets.text: Flint 0.3.0 adds dynamic chart widgets that switch chart types and edit chart properties in place.

release022.text: Flint 0.2.2 added compact dodge modes and grouped violin layouts.

release021.text: Flint 0.2.1 improved chart-property validation and backend consistency.

landing.howItWorksBody: Flint starts with a compact spec: the data, semantic types, and the chart spec. From there, the compiler produces a complete backend-native spec (shown here in Vega-Lite) filling with the necessary low-level details and renders a good-looking chart.
landing.overviewAlt: Flint workflow: an agent infers a dataSpec from a raw table, a short chartSpec is written, and Flint compiles it into a faceted line chart, then a grouped bar, waterfall, heatmap, and sunburst as the spec is edited.
landing.leadBefore: Flint is a visualization intermediate language that lets
landing.leadHighlight1: AI agents reliably create expressive, good-looking charts from simple, human-editable chart specs
landing.leadMiddle: . Instead of requiring verbose low-level parameters such as scales, axes, spacing, and layout, the Flint compiler derives optimized chart settings from the data, semantic types, chart type, and encodings.
landing.leadHighlight2: Flint supports {{chartTypes}} chart types across {{backends}} rendering backends through one unified interface
landing.closingBody: Open source and ready to use. Start from GitHub or browse examples in the gallery.
landing.closingCollab: Flint is built by <msr>Microsoft Research</msr> in collaboration with the <ideas>IDEAS Lab</ideas>, Renmin University of China.

semantic.title: Specify with semantic types
semantic.body: Flint uses semantic types to capture meanings of data fields (e.g., Rank, YearMonth, Delta, Temperature), and uses them to infer the low-level chart configuration like parsing, scale, axes, formatting and color schemes.
semantic.example: For this heatmap of net new users gains by game and month, Flint determines the temporal value parser, axis formatting, and diverging color scheme and midpoint based on the semantic types of the fields.

layout.title: Automatic layout optimization
layout.body: Flint optimizes the chart layout based on an elastic layout model and banking principles. The compiler dynamically manages sizing, spacing, and arrangement so the chart nicely fits into the canvas.
layout.example: As the grouped bar chart number increases, Flint stretches the canvas and reduces the band width so the dense version still fits the canvas nicely, similar to how springs settle into an expandable container.

adapt.title: Easy to generate and adapt
adapt.body: Without fragile low-level parameters, Flint specs can be easily generated and adapted by users. Changing a chart design requires only switching the chart type and rebinding visual encodings, and the compiler cascades the new encoding choices to the low-level settings.
adapt.example: The user can easily turn a faceted bar chart of the 2000 U.S. Census population distribution by gender and age into a pyramid chart by switching the chart type. The compiler handles the rest.

backends.title: Render with different backends
backends.body: Flint supports {{chartTypes}} chart types across Vega-Lite, ECharts, Chart.js, and Plotly, with {{examples}} backend-specific examples in the gallery, and can emit native Excel charts through Office.js. Despite their different APIs and programming models, Flint hides them behind a unified interface.
backends.example: Switch backends to use their native strengths: ECharts for hierarchical sunbursts, Plotly for statistical and analytical traces, or Excel for editable charts embedded in a workbook.

themes.title: Render with different themes
themes.body: A Flint theme is a formal specification, not a cosmetic skin. It guides the layout algorithm, applies presentation rules by semantic role, and defines geometry, typography, and color as one visual system.
themes.example: The same grouped-bar spec becomes an Economist print graphic or a Swiss typographic composition. The data and encodings stay fixed while the compiler changes spacing, structure, labels, marks, type, and color.

mcp.heroTitle: Use Flint as an MCP server for your agent
mcp.leadAfter: server and your agent can create charts as an interactive MCP app. By default it opens an interactive Flint chart view; when you need artifacts, it can also return static images or backend-native specs.
mcp.quickStartBody: paste this setup request into your agent and let it configure Flint for the current project. For manual setup, see
mcp.localSetupBody: Recommended if your client supports local MCP
mcp.remoteSetupBody: Use if your client only supports remote MCP
mcp.experienceBody: Using Flint through MCP is a simple loop: connect the server, ask for the chart you want, and work with a visualization with dynamic widgets provided by the MCP server.
mcp.step1Body: Add the stdio server to your MCP client. The agent can chart local CSV, TSV, or JSON files by default.
mcp.step2Body: The agent turns your request into one Flint spec, chooses the chart type and fields, then calls the MCP server to validate and render it.
mcp.step3Body: In hosts with MCP Apps, the preferred tool opens a live SVG preview with chart options. When an artifact is needed, Flint can return a PNG, SVG, or compiled backend spec instead.
mcp.providesBody: The server keeps the tool surface small: one preferred interactive tool, supporting tools for static render and validation, plus resources that teach the agent Flint's chart vocabulary.
mcp.installBody: For manual setup, the server speaks stdio and runs zero-install with npx. Point your MCP client at the package:
mcp.dataBody: Tool calls can embed rows directly with data.values. The agent can also chart a local CSV, TSV, or JSON file by data.url out of the box. Remote URLs are never fetched. For an untrusted deployment, pass --disable-file-reference to reject local file references and accept only inline data.values:
mcp.referenceBody: The docs cover the full MCP workflow. The package README is the shortest reference for tool inputs, CLI flags, and client config.
mcp.skillNote: Adding Flint to your own app? The standalone <skillLink>Flint Agent Skill</skillLink> teaches coding agents to author specs and integrate Flint.

tools.create_chart_view: Opens the interactive MCP App: live SVG preview plus chart options. Use this whenever the user wants to see a chart.
tools.render_chart: Returns a static PNG or SVG. Use it when the host has no App UI, or when the user asks for an image artifact.
tools.compile_chart: Returns the backend-native spec JSON for Vega-Lite, ECharts, or Chart.js, along with assembly warnings.
tools.validate_chart: Checks whether a spec is valid, reports warnings or errors, and returns the computed chart size.
tools.list_chart_types: Lists chart types and encoding channels, optionally scoped to one backend.
tools.agentSkill: Bundled authoring instructions for producing valid ChartAssemblyInput specs.
tools.chartTypes: A browsable catalog of chart types and encoding channels across all backends.
tools.authorPrompt: Loads the Flint authoring skill in prompt-aware clients before chart tool calls.
